lesson.title: Energy in the Electric Field: How Much a Capacitor Can Deliver
lesson.summary: Charging a capacitor stores real, recoverable energy in its electric field, following E equals one half C V squared.
lesson.body:
A capacitor does not just hold charge, it holds energy, and that energy is exactly what you get back when the capacitor discharges through a circuit. Pulling opposite charges apart onto the two plates takes work, in the same sense that stretching a spring or lifting a weight against gravity takes work, and that work does not vanish, it is stored in the electric field between the plates until something gives the charge a path to flow back together.

You can see where the energy formula comes from by thinking about the charging process step by step. Early in charging, the plates hold little charge and the voltage across them is low, so pushing the first bit of charge onto the plates costs very little work. As charging continues, the accumulated charge raises the voltage, following V equals Q divided by C, so each additional bit of charge costs more work than the last. Because voltage climbs in direct proportion to charge, the average voltage over the whole charging process is exactly halfway between zero and the final voltage V, meaning the average is V divided by 2. Total work equals that average voltage multiplied by the total charge moved, Q, and since Q equals C times V, the energy stored works out to one half times C times V squared, written E equals one half C V squared, with E in joules, C in farads, and V in volts.

Try it with a capacitor you would actually find on a circuit board: a 470 microfarad electrolytic capacitor charged to 16 volts, a common combination in power supply filtering. First square the voltage: 16 squared is 256. Multiply by the capacitance: 470 times 10 to the negative sixth farads, times 256, equals 120,320 times 10 to the negative sixth, or 0.12032. Finally take half of that: 0.12032 divided by 2 equals 0.06016 joules, or 60.16 millijoules. That is a modest amount of energy, but it is enough to hold a logic circuit's supply voltage steady through a brief power interruption, which is exactly what filter capacitors are doing in most electronics.

Scale the same formula up and the applications change dramatically. A camera flash charges a capacitor rated in the hundreds of microfarads up to a few hundred volts over a second or two, and because energy grows with the square of voltage, that higher voltage lets a physically compact capacitor store several joules, enough to drive a genuinely bright flash tube for a fraction of a millisecond when discharged all at once. At the far end of the scale, supercapacitors with values measured in whole farads store energy comparable to a small battery, used for things like holding memory during a power blip or delivering a brief burst of high current.

The key distinction to carry forward is that a capacitor stores energy without converting it to heat, unlike a resistor, which only ever dissipates the electrical energy passing through it as heat and gives none of it back. Charge a capacitor and then disconnect the source, and the energy calculated by one half C V squared sits there, recoverable, until you give the charge somewhere to go, whether that is a flash tube, an LED, or simply the rest of the circuit it is embedded in.
